Read About La Paz

The highest seat of government on Earth, strung down a canyon wall by cable car — and why the altitude is the least strange thing about it.

A city that shouldn't work, and does

La Paz is not, technically, Bolivia's capital. That honor belongs to Sucre, a colonial city several hundred kilometers to the southeast, which keeps the country's judiciary and its constitutional claim to the title. But the presidency, the legislature, and every foreign embassy in the country sit in La Paz, which makes it the capital in every way that matters to a traveler, and which makes the technicality a piece of trivia Bolivians enjoy watching visitors get wrong.

What is not trivia is the altitude. La Paz's city center sits at roughly 3,640 meters — about 11,940 feet — which makes it the highest seat of national government anywhere in the world, and its neighbor city El Alto, perched on the rim above, climbs past 4,100 meters. At that height the air holds roughly 40% less oxygen than it does at sea level. Most visitors feel it within the first hour: a shortness of breath climbing stairs, a mild headache, an odd fatigue that has nothing to do with jet lag. It passes for most people within a day or two. Coca leaf tea — mate de coca, served in every hotel lobby in the city — is the local remedy, offered without ceremony because everyone needs it at first. Arrive with low expectations for your first afternoon, drink water aggressively, skip the pisco sour until day two, and the city stops fighting you fairly quickly.

A city built into a hole

Most capitals sit on plains or rivers. La Paz sits inside a canyon, and that fact organizes everything about how the city works and how it feels to move through it. The Spanish founded it in 1548 in a river gorge specifically because the terrain offered shelter from the wind and a break from the brutal, exposed cold of the surrounding altiplano — the high plateau that stretches toward Lake Titicaca and the Peruvian border. What they got in exchange for that shelter was a city with almost no flat ground, built instead on a canyon wall that drops nearly 900 meters from rim to river.

Altitude in La Paz isn't just a number on a sign. It's the organizing principle of the entire social geography.

That elevation drop turned into the city's defining social fact: in La Paz, unlike almost anywhere else, wealth runs downhill. The lower you go, the warmer and more oxygen-rich the air becomes, and the more expensive the real estate. The Zona Sur, the southern valley neighborhoods at the canyon's lowest point, holds the city's mansions, embassies, and shopping malls. The historic center and the working-class hillside barrios climb upward from there, thinning out in air and income until they reach El Alto, the sister city on the canyon rim, which is poorer, colder, and overwhelmingly indigenous Aymara. El Alto didn't exist as its own city until 1985; today it has grown larger in population than La Paz itself, the fastest-growing city in South America for much of the 2000s.

The cable cars that fixed a broken commute

For most of La Paz's history, the trip between the canyon floor and El Alto's rim meant a punishing bus ride on switchback roads that could take well over an hour in traffic, made worse by a topography no metro or tram could ever be dug through. In 2014, the government opened Mi Teleférico, an urban cable car network that now carries more than 300,000 riders a day across ten interconnected lines — the largest urban aerial cable car system in the world by a wide margin.

It is, unusually for a piece of transit infrastructure, also one of the best things to do in the city. The cars glide silently over rooftops and canyon walls, turning a daily commute into a panoramic ride that most tourist gondolas charge admission for. From the Red Line's cars you can watch the city's entire vertical society scroll past in a few minutes: the colonial center, the brick barrios climbing the slope, and finally El Alto's flat, sprawling grid on the rim, with the snow-capped bulk of Illimani — the 6,438-meter peak that watches over the whole valley — visible on a clear day from almost any car.

El Alto and the architecture of new wealth

El Alto has its own recent architectural signature, and it is impossible to miss once you know to look for it: the cholets, a portmanteau of "chalet" and cholo (a term for Bolivia's indigenous and mestizo population, reclaimed here with pride). These are flamboyant, multi-story buildings — part event hall, part apartment block, part family mansion — wrapped in bright geometric facades inspired by Tiwanaku textile patterns and Andean color symbolism. More than sixty now dot El Alto's skyline.

They are the work of Freddy Mamani, a self-taught architect and the son of an indigenous market family, who began designing them in the early 2000s as newly prosperous Aymara business families — many who had made fortunes in trade, transport, and construction after decades of exclusion from the city below — wanted homes that announced their success on their own cultural terms rather than European ones. Architecture critics abroad took notice; Mamani's buildings have been exhibited in Paris and written up in the international design press as a genuine indigenous modernism, not a folk curiosity. Locally, they are simply a sign that El Alto's money no longer needs La Paz's permission to be visible.

The Aymara nation the Spanish never fully absorbed

La Paz and El Alto sit at the heart of Aymara country, and the Aymara — unlike many indigenous nations elsewhere in the hemisphere — were never demographically overwhelmed by colonization. They remain the majority population across much of the Bolivian altiplano, with their own language, their own Andean cosmology, and a visible, unapologetic public culture. The bowler hats worn by cholitas — Aymara and Quechua women in voluminous pollera skirts, woven shawls, and gold jewelry — are not a costume for tourists; the style descends from a hat British railway workers reportedly brought to Bolivia in the 1920s, adopted and made entirely their own.

That same confidence now extends to spectacle: cholita wrestling, staged most weekends in El Alto's arenas, puts these women in the ring as full-throated luchadoras, flipping opponents in their traditional dress to crowds that treat it as both sport and cultural statement. It reads, correctly, as neither parody nor performance for outsiders — it is Aymara women claiming a stage that was never built for them and making it entirely theirs.

Tiwanaku, and a civilization older than the Inca

Long before the Inca reached this stretch of the altiplano, the Tiwanaku civilization built a monumental urban and ceremonial center on the shores of Lake Titicaca, about seventy kilometers from present-day La Paz. At its peak between roughly 500 and 1000 CE, Tiwanaku was the religious and political capital of an empire that stretched across parts of modern Bolivia, Peru, and Chile — centuries before the Inca even existed as a distinct polity. The Inca themselves regarded Tiwanaku's ruins as the work of giants or gods, and folded its origin myths into their own.

The precision stonework at the site — gateways cut from single blocks of andesite, aligned with equinox sunrises with an accuracy that still puzzles archaeologists — is now a UNESCO World Heritage site and one of the most significant pre-Columbian ruins on the continent. It is also a reminder that the altiplano's political and architectural sophistication long predates Spanish arrival, and even predates the empire most visitors associate with Andean South America.

A revolution, a coup, and a first

Bolivia's twentieth century ran through La Paz's streets more than once. The 1952 Bolivian National Revolution — a genuine social upheaval that nationalized the country's tin mines, granted universal suffrage, and broke up the semi-feudal hacienda system that had kept indigenous Bolivians as agricultural serfs — began here and reshaped the country's politics for a generation. Instability followed for decades afterward, including a string of military governments and, in 1980, a particularly brutal coup that briefly made Bolivia synonymous internationally with narco-trafficking and human rights abuses.

The most consequential change came in 2006, when Evo Morales, an Aymara former coca-growers' union leader, took office as Bolivia's first indigenous president — in a country where the indigenous majority had been governed almost exclusively by a criollo and mestizo elite since colonization. Whatever one makes of his subsequent fourteen years in power, which ended in disputed elections and his exile in 2019, the symbolic weight of that first inauguration in La Paz is hard to overstate: the Aymara and Quechua majority, visible everywhere in the city's markets and streets, finally held the country's highest office too.

Why to go anyway

La Paz will never be an easy city to love in the way Lisbon or Buenos Aires are easy to love. It is exhausting in the most literal, physiological sense before it is anything else. But few cities anywhere offer this particular combination: a functioning, modern capital of nearly two million people, built into a canyon so steep that cable cars are its metro system, surrounded by an indigenous majority culture that was never erased and never asked anyone's permission to keep being itself. Illimani stands over all of it, visible from a teleférico car or a rooftop bar on any clear morning, entirely indifferent to the altitude sickness of whoever happens to be looking up at it that day.
